constraints: s and t contain lowercase English letters only.

examples.explain: Same letters, different counts: s has two a's, t has one.

hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when their letters, sorted, are identical. What does sorting cost?
Instead of sorting, count. What should the counts look like for anagrams?
Add 1 for each letter of s and subtract 1 for each letter of t. Anagrams leave every count at 0.

insight.mnemonic: Same bag of letters, different order.
insight.oneLiner: Anagrams have identical letter counts - count up for s, down for t, and check everything cancels.

recall.a: A set forgets multiplicity: 'aab' and 'abb' have the same set of letters.
recall.q: Why is a set comparison not enough?
What's the space cost of the counting solution for lowercase input?

insight.why: Counting is O(n) with at most 26 keys, beating the O(n log n) sort. The length check up front rejects the easy cases.

oneLiner: Anagrams have identical letter counts - count up for s, down for t, and check everything cancels.

pitfalls.explain: set(s) == set(t) ignores how many times each letter appears ('aab' vs 'abb').
pitfalls.title: Compared sets of letters

pitfalls.explain: If t is longer than s, checking only s's letters against t can wrongly pass.
pitfalls.title: Skipped the length check

solutions.idea: Sorting is a canonical form: two anagrams sort to the same string.
solutions.name: Sort both strings

footnotes.text: One dict and one pass. If both strings use the same multiset of letters, every +1 meets a matching −1.

solutions.idea: One pass that adds for s and subtracts for t. Every count must return to zero.
solutions.name: Count letters

starter:
class Solution:
    def isAnagram(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
statement: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an **anagram** of `s`: the same letters, each used the same number of times, possibly in a different order. Otherwise return `false`.
title: Valid Anagram
